solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Scottish mixed grain, potatoes and chopped meat

indicators.note: something chopped has had its end cut off, so the meat word loses its last letter

blocks.note: mash is mashed potatoes
lamb is a meat

explanation.surface: A Scottish recipe listing grain, potatoes and chopped meat.
explanation.walkthrough: MASH + LAM(B). MASHLAM (or mashlum) is a Scots word for a mixture of grains, such as maslin.
explanation.definitionFit: Mashlam is a Scottish dialect word for mixed grain, wheat and rye or oats and barley sown together.

clue.text: Guys with spades are on the loose with intent to commit crime

indicators.note: things on the loose are free and scattered, so these letters are let out of their order

blocks.note: guys are men
S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Men carrying spades roam about, plainly up to no good.
explanation.walkthrough: MENS REA is the legal Latin for 'guilty mind', the mental element of a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, mens rea is the guilty mind, the criminal intention that must accompany the act.

clue.text: Make good guess after one

indicators.note: after places the guess word second, behind the word for one, so the order is flipped from the clue

blocks.note: a means one
'I bet' means I guess

explanation.surface: A tip for winning: make a good guess after the first try.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after one' puts BET after A. 'Make good' is an old Spenserian sense of ABET, to maintain or uphold.
explanation.definitionFit: In obsolete usage abet meant to maintain or back up, a sense recorded in Chambers as make good.

clue.text: Soldier runs into husband flourishing Irish dagger

indicators.note: running into a place means getting inside it, so the soldier goes within the other letters
flourishing suggests something waved about wildly, so these letters are tossed out of order

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier
taken as written, then rearranged around the soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier bursts in on a husband who is brandishing a dagger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'husband' looks like a person in the scene but is the anagram fodder. The SGIAN DUBH is the knife tucked in a Highland stocking; Chambers glosses it as Gaelic, Irish or Scottish.
explanation.definitionFit: A sgian dubh, Gaelic for 'black knife', is a small dagger of the Gaels, worn in the stocking.

clue.text: Nothing excluded from restructured US model plants

indicators.note: excluded means left out, so the round letter for nothing is dropped from the fodder
restructured means rebuilt in a new form, so the remaining letters are put in a fresh order

blocks.note: nothing is zero, the round letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A redesigned American model has dropped something, and now it produces plants.
explanation.walkthrough: Take O out of US MODEL and rearrange what remains. Ledum is the genus of Labrador tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Ledums are evergreen shrubs of the heath family, such as Labrador tea, so they are plants.

clue.text: Woven fabrics fit young women

blocks.note: to mate is to match or fit together
lasses are girls

explanation.surface: Woven cloth suits girls well, or so a fashion note might say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fit' reads as an adjective about the fabrics, but it is a verb, to match or pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Matelasse is a heavy fabric woven with a raised, quilted-looking pattern, so the plural names such cloths.

clue.text: Sound stance finishes off Cambridge exams

indicators.note: taking the finishes off means each of the two words loses its final letter

blocks.note: trig is a Scots word for neat, trim and sound
a pose is a stance

explanation.surface: A firm stance finally sees a student through the Cambridge exams.
explanation.walkthrough: TRI(G) + POS(E). 'Sound' looks like a noise or homophone signal; here it is the adjective, healthy or trim.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tripos is the honours degree examination at Cambridge University, each subject having its own.

clue.text: Cut climbing plant, not very short

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to leave out the next thing named, removing it from the plant word

blocks.note: vetch is a climbing leguminous plant
V is the short form of very

explanation.surface: Instructions to prune a climbing plant, but not too much.
explanation.walkthrough: VETCH loses V. 'very short' means very in its abbreviated form.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to cut lines into a surface, as with acid on a metal plate.

clue.text: Old huge type, not entirely pretentious

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the next word is used, a run of its letters

blocks.note: the run of letters sitting in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: An old style of typeface, large and a touch pretentious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'huge type' suggests large print; it means a kind of huge being, a giant.
explanation.definitionFit: Eten (or ettin) is an archaic word for a giant, so an old term for a huge type of being.

clue.text: One wanted charge by weight for French fabric

indicators.note: wanted in the sense of lacking, so the word for charge lacks the letter for one

blocks.note: a means one
something in your care is in your charge
a tonne is a metric weight

explanation.surface: A wanted man is charged by weight for some French cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One wanted' looks like a fugitive; in fact the letter for one is what the charge word wants, or lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Cretonne is a strong printed cotton fabric for upholstery, named from Creton in Normandy.

clue.text: Right away, poor called to account

indicators.note: away means gone, so the letter for right is taken out

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
hard up means short of money

explanation.surface: Fair enough: a poor person was summoned to explain himself.
explanation.walkthrough: HARD UP without R. 'Right away' reads as 'at once'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be had up is to be brought before a court or authority to answer a charge, an informal idiom.

clue.text: American edentates cross ground near hart

indicators.note: ground as in milled or crushed, so these letters are broken up and remade

blocks.note: X is the shape of a cross
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Toothless American animals cross the ground close to a deer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' reads as land underfoot; it is the past tense of grind. Edentates are toothless mammals.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenarthra is the order of New World mammals including sloths, anteaters and armadillos, formerly called edentates.

clue.text: That's number recalled first from Louis Armstrong?

indicators.note: recalled as in called back, so the first words are read in the opposite direction
'first from' keeps only the first letter of 'Louis'

blocks.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is
N is short for number
the opening letter of Louis

explanation.surface: A trivia question asking which song a jazz great recorded first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Louis Armstrong' steers to jazz; the definition is just 'Armstrong?', the question mark flagging a different one.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Armstrong, the first man on the Moon, shares a surname with the trumpeter Louis Armstrong.

clue.text: Adult and youngster in ruffled lace — that's the Spanish way

indicators.note: 'in' places the adult and youngster inside the other letters
ruffled means disordered, so the letters of the lace are disturbed

blocks.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
a minor is someone under age
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A grown-up and a child in frilly lace, dressed for a Spanish occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: The adult and youngster go into the middle of the jumbled lace, not at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Camino real is Spanish for 'royal road', the name given to the old highways of Spain and its empire.

clue.text: Couple regretted leaving university in rows

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so the letter for university goes out of the word

blocks.note: to tie is to couple or join
rued means regretted
U is short for university

explanation.surface: A pair regretted dropping out of university amid quarrels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rows' sounds like quarrels here, but it means lines, as of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiered means arranged in layers or rows one above another, like seats in a theatre.

clue.text: Old sculpture to flog in America after centre's moved to the front

indicators.note: 'in' puts the flogging word inside the country's letters

indicators.text: after centre's moved to the front
indicators.note: the middle letter of the country is shifted to the start, changing its position

blocks.note: tat is a dialect verb meaning to whip or flog
the United States of America

explanation.surface: Selling an old statue in the States once the middle has been rearranged.
explanation.walkthrough: The centre letter of the country's abbreviation moves to its front before the flogging word goes inside. Tat is a dialect verb, to whip; STATUA is the old word for statue.
explanation.definitionFit: Statua is an archaic form of statue, used by Shakespeare, so an old sculpture.

clue.text: One remedying great ills?

indicators.note: remedying means putting right, so the letters are set in a corrected order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor who treats serious illnesses.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay at once; the question mark admits that allergies are not always great ills.
explanation.definitionFit: An allergist is a doctor specialising in diagnosing and treating allergies, which can be serious illnesses.

clue.text: Lively tune followed by tenor

blocks.note: ran after, as in followed a course
T is the abbreviation for tenor, placed by the verb

explanation.surface: A merry tune comes next, sung by a tenor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'followed by' looks like a single link, but 'followed' supplies RAN. A rant is a lively Scottish dance tune.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, a rant is a lively, rollicking tune or the boisterous dance done to it.

clue.text: Yarrow, for example may be seen in a cold river

blocks.note: taken as written
a chill is a cold
ea is a dialect word for a river or stream

explanation.surface: Yarrow, the wild plant, might grow along a cold stream.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yarrow' is also a Scottish river, which pulls toward the wordplay; it is the plant here.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarrow is Achillea millefolium, so it is an example of the genus Achillea of flowering plants.

clue.text: Unfinished brass work in lounge

indicators.note: unfinished means lacking its end, so the money word loses its final letter

blocks.note: brass and lolly are both slang for money
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A half-done brass sculpture sits in the lounge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brass' looks like the metal, but in British slang it means money, as does lolly.
explanation.definitionFit: To lollop is to lounge or loll about idly, as well as to bound clumsily.

clue.text: Clobber I'd cast? Yes

indicators.note: to clobber is to batter, so these letters are knocked into a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A performer confirms that she would throw off her clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' is British slang for clothes, so the whole clue reads as a stripper agreeing to shed them, while also working as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecdysiast, coined by H. L. Mencken from the Greek for moulting, is a jocular word for a striptease artist.

clue.text: Short passage put across time and time again in fast codas

indicators.note: short means cut back, so the passage word loses its final letter
put across means laid over and around, so the passage word straddles the times

blocks.note: a street is a passage or thoroughfare
T is short for time, given twice

explanation.surface: A brief musical passage repeated again and again in fast endings.
explanation.walkthrough: STREE(T) goes around TT. Stretta is the Italian term for a closing section played faster; strette is its plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretta is a final passage taken at a quicker tempo, so strette are fast codas.

clue.text: Aware agreement includes half of Bath?

indicators.note: includes means takes inside, so the agreement word wraps around the other part
half of means only one of the word's two halves is used

blocks.note: consent is agreement
Bath is a city; the first half of city

explanation.surface: A conscious agreement covering half the spa town of Bath.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that Bath is defined by example: it is a CITY, and half of that word is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Conscient is an old word for conscious, so it means aware.

clue.text: House fruit

blocks.note: first meaning: the Dutch royal house of ...-Nassau
second meaning: the citrus fruit

explanation.walkthrough: 'House fruit' reads like a fruit grown indoors; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Orange names both the princely dynasty of the Netherlands and the familiar citrus fruit.

clue.text: PC up on haunt of vice in part of London

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means read from bottom to top, so the computer word turns around

blocks.note: a Mac is an Apple personal computer
a den of iniquity is a haunt of vice

explanation.surface: A police constable heads into a London borough's red-light district.
explanation.walkthrough: PC looks like a police constable, but it is a personal computer, an Apple one here.
explanation.definitionFit: Camden is a borough of north London, known for its market and Camden Town.

clue.text: Sweeper and boiler needing repair

indicators.note: something needing repair is broken, so its letters are to be reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: The house's chimney sweep and the broken boiler both want fixing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweeper' suggests cleaning, but it is the football position.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a libero, or sweeper, is a free defender who plays behind the back line.

clue.text: Grey storyteller beginning to drag

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, which is all that is used

blocks.note: a liar tells stories
the opening letter of drag

explanation.surface: A dull storyteller starts to drag on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storyteller' is a mild euphemism for a liar.
explanation.definitionFit: Liard is an old word, chiefly Scots, for grey or dapple-grey, especially of a horse.

clue.text: Relative about to get into Britain

indicators.note: getting into somewhere means being inside it, so the 'about' word goes within the other letters

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
BR is an abbreviation for Britain

explanation.surface: A family member is about to be allowed into Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' looks like 'soon going to'; 'about' is RE and 'to get into' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Brer is a dialect form of brother, familiar from Brer Rabbit, so it names a relative.

clue.text: Eddy's refrain heard

indicators.note: heard means received by ear, so a word with the same sound is wanted

blocks.note: a wheel is a refrain or chorus of a song

explanation.surface: Eddy's song chorus can be heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eddy' looks like a man's name; it is a swirl of water. 'refrain' is a noun, not 'hold back'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wiel (or weel) is a Scots word for a whirlpool, so a small eddy in water.

clue.text: One leaving country before tackling fighter

indicators.note: tackling suggests grabbing hold around, so the 'before' word wraps the fighter

blocks.note: ere is a poetic word for before
a MiG is a Russian fighter plane

explanation.surface: An emigrant fights his way out before tackling a fighter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' looks like a time word linking the parts, but it supplies ERE.
explanation.definitionFit: An emigre is a person who has left their own country, usually for political reasons.

clue.text: Robbed once by force in return

indicators.note: 'in' places the force letter inside the other abbreviation

blocks.note: F is the symbol for force in physics
ret. is an abbreviation for return

explanation.surface: Robbed by force long ago, in retaliation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in return' reads as 'in exchange'; 'in' is the container signal and 'return' gives RET.
explanation.definitionFit: Reft is an old past participle of reave, to rob or plunder, hence robbed in older English.

clue.text: Plan leaving German out of the corporation

indicators.note: out means removed, so the letter for German is taken away
to plan is to arrange, so the letters are laid out anew

blocks.note: taken as written
G is short for German

explanation.surface: A scheme to quit Germany and leave the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporation' looks like a company, but jocularly it means a paunch. 'leaving' is the fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Alvine means relating to the belly or intestines, and a corporation is a humorous word for a big belly.

clue.text: Conference stamp on source of taxes

indicators.note: a source is where something begins, so only the opening letter is used

blocks.note: a die is a stamp for striking coins
the opening letter of taxes

explanation.surface: A conference puts its stamp on where taxes come from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' places DIE before T, as in a down-the-page or left-to-right join.
explanation.definitionFit: A diet is a formal assembly or legislative conference, as in the Diet of Worms or Japan's Diet.

clue.text: Turncoats see danger all over the place

indicators.note: something all over the place is scattered in disorder, so these letters are mixed

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Traitors spot peril wherever they look.
explanation.definitionFit: Renegades desert their side or cause for another, which is what turncoats do.

clue.text: Writer Pound fooled about

indicators.note: about as in turned about, so the combined letters face the other way

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra
to be had is to be fooled

explanation.surface: The poet Ezra Pound played the fool for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer Pound' points at Ezra Pound; the writer is a different one, Roald Dahl.
explanation.definitionFit: Roald Dahl was a British writer of children's books such as Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.

clue.text: Rubber packing-ring wrapped round clear watchglass

indicators.note: wrapped round means enclosing, so the ring word surrounds the next word

blocks.note: a lute is a rubber ring sealing a jar lid
net, as in net profit, means clear of deductions

explanation.surface: A rubber seal is fitted round a clear glass on a watch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clear' looks like transparent glass; it means net.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunette is a flattened watch glass, among its other crescent-shaped senses.
